title: After the Lagos Okada Ban, MAX Moved From Rides to Vehicle Loans
dek: When Lagos barred commercial motorcycles from its busiest areas in 2020, MAX kept hiring, leaned on other cities and turned its rider loans into the business.

story.event: Responding to the 2020 Lagos ban on commercial motorcycles by shifting from bike-hailing towards vehicle financing
story.summary: On 27 January 2020 Lagos announced that from 1 February commercial motorcycles and tricycles would be barred from major roads in six local government areas, hitting MAX, the bike-hailing company founded by Adetayo Bamiduro and Chinedu Azodoh, which financed riders' bikes. MAX kept hiring, moved part of its fleet into deliveries and grew in other cities, and by December 2021, when it raised a $31 million Series B, described itself as a vehicle subscription and financing platform. In January 2025 it laid off about 150 staff as it moved to financing only electric vehicles.
paragraphs: On Monday 27 January 2020, Lagos State announced that from 1 February commercial motorcycles and tricycles would be barred from major roads, bridges and highways in six local government areas and 15 council development areas, for safety and security. Hospitals had recorded more than 10,000 accidents from 2016 to 2019, said the information commissioner, Gbenga Omotoso. The ban covered "all forms of motorcycles", said the transport commissioner. That included MAX, the bike-hailing company Adetayo Bamiduro and Chinedu Azodoh had founded in 2015.

MAX said it was exempt, its bikes being 220cc, above the 200cc limit in a 2018 state law. It had also become a lender. Banks would not lend to riders, Azodoh said in late 2019, and microfinance banks charged 7 to 10 per cent a month, so MAX financed bikes costing about $1,700, repaid daily. About 1,250 riders had such loans by late 2019. Bamiduro said the ban could affect up to 2,000 riders, and that MAX had put close to $10 million into Lagos, over $5 million of it in loans.

Gokada, a rival that worked only in Lagos, laid off many of its staff and turned to deliveries. Bamiduro took another course. "MAX.ng is actually hiring more people, we are not laying off anybody," he said in mid-February. MAX was already in four cities and could still serve most of Lagos. It moved a significant part of its fleet into deliveries, which it said at least doubled by July, and pushed growth in Kano, Ibadan and Akure. Bamiduro now described MAX as infrastructure for moving people and goods, not "okada transport or okada delivery".

Over the next two years the loans became the business. By December 2021, when it raised a $31 million Series B after more than $40 million of driver-financing debt, MAX called itself a vehicle subscription platform, offering motorcycles, tricycles and cars, some electric, on rent-to-own terms, with a lease-to-own scheme for Bolt drivers. In 2022 Bamiduro called the Lagos rules "momentarily a challenge for us, but fundamentally not a challenge for long." In January 2025 MAX laid off about 150 people, 30 per cent of its workforce, TechCabal reported, as it moved to financing only electric vehicles. "This decision was not made lightly," the company said.

quote.text: do all things as one that remembereth the days coming after, when speech availeth not.
quote.source_title: The Instruction of Ptah-Hotep and the Instruction of Ke'Gemni, tr. Battiscombe G. Gunn, Project Gutenberg eBook #30508
quote.connection: Ptahhotep tells a leader to act as one who remembers the days to come, when words will no longer help. MAX argued its case hard in January 2020, but argument did not lift the ban; what carried the company was what it had built beforehand: other cities, deliveries and a book of riders' loans.

reflection: Some days a decision made by someone else, a ministry, a funder, a manager, lands on work you have done carefully and within the rules. It is fair to say so plainly, and MAX did. But argument has a short reach once the decision is made.

What lasted for MAX was the work that did not depend on one city's permission. You might ask, without alarm, which part of your own week rests on a single person's yes. Most good work has some of that. The point is to know where it sits, and to keep one other thing growing quietly beside it.
invitation: Name one part of your work or income that depends on a single decision you do not control. Write down one small thing already within your reach that would still stand if that decision went the other way.

cross_checks.claim: Lagos barred commercial motorcycles and tricycles from major roads in six local government areas from 1 February 2020.
MAX said its bikes were 220cc, above the 200cc exemption in the 2018 Lagos law.
Before the ban MAX already financed riders' bikes, repaid in daily amounts, and had put millions of dollars into loans for operators in Lagos.
Gokada, which operated only in Lagos, laid off staff and turned to logistics after the ban.
In December 2021 MAX raised a $31 million Series B as a vehicle subscription and financing platform, after more than $40 million in driver-financing debt.
In January 2025 MAX laid off about 150 staff, about 30 per cent, as it moved to financing only electric vehicles.

research_notes: Episode framing: the slate says MAX 'turned to vehicle financing after Lagos banned motorcycle taxis', but MAX already financed riders' bikes before the ban (hire purchase from 2017 per TechCabal 2020; 'introduced vehicle financing in 2018' per TechCrunch 2021; Azodoh's November 2019 interview). The story therefore tells the ban as the moment the financing side, already present, became the core business over the following two years, and does not claim the ban alone caused it. Ban scope: six LGAs and 15 LCDAs (WeeTracker, quoting the government's announcement); TechCabal says six areas; Nairametrics says 15 local governments; Bamiduro told WeeTracker MAX could still work in 15 of 21 LGAs. The story uses six local government areas and 15 council development areas. Rider numbers: about 1,250 financed riders by late 2019 (Azodoh in TechCabal, November 2019; Bamiduro in TechCabal, July 2020) versus 'up to 2,000 riders on our platform' (Bamiduro to Nairametrics, February 2020) and 2,200 direct jobs including staff (MAX statement via WeeTracker); both rider figures are given with who said them. Bolt: TechCrunch (2021) describes a lease-to-own arrangement intended for 10,000 Bolt drivers, and Bamiduro (TechCabal 2022) said MAX provided subscriptions to at least 10,000 Bolt drivers while also giving a total of 'over 8,000 vehicle subscriptions'; because these conflict, the story mentions the Bolt scheme without numbers. Layoffs: TechCabal's figure of about 150 (30%) comes from two people familiar with the company; MAX declined to give a number; the story attributes the figure to TechCabal. Lead investors for the Series B are given as Lightrock alone in some reports and as Lightrock with Global Ventures in TechCrunch and Techweez; not used in the story. Funding kept as 'venture' (equity from Novastar, Lightrock, Global Ventures and others), noting that much of the lending capital was institutional debt. The government's case (accidents and security) is given in its own words; MAX's claim that the ban broke the state's own law is reported as the company's statement, without judging it. Several TechCabal pages refuse the WebFetch tool but load for the checker and were read in full with a plain request. Ptahhotep's line comes from Maxim 16, addressed to a leader enforcing rules; the excerpt begins mid-sentence.
